prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration: a single prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. After the full exchange, what carries it for me is not the count of supporters, which the chair rightly says is partly convergence, but three things I can check. First, the physical idea is distinct: magic-wavelength trapping lets many atoms be interrogated with the dominant motional and light-shift systematics removed, which is not the frequency comb and not the single-ion clock. Second, the central result is a measured quantity that does not wait for future payoffs: uncertainties and instabilities near 1e-18 reproduced and cross-compared by independent laboratories over fibre links. That is the kind of quantitative, reproducible agreement between theory-level understanding and measured spectra that I trust most. Third, the credit is the most separable on the list: Katori proposed the scheme and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye took it to record accuracy and coherence, with the JILA strontium evaluations and later many-body, degenerate-gas operation. I would word the citation around the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping so that it neither repeats the 2005 comb prize nor pre-empts any later recognition of a nuclear clock.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that this is a metrological achievement whose fundamental-physics payoff (constants, dark matter, relativistic geodesy) is still largely prospective, and it sits next to the 2005 and 2012 prizes. A committee that wants a newly verified state of matter would find B021 or B024 a closer fit to my own field. I have weighed that and conclude that B021 still carries an attribution gap (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan) and B024 still has an open pairing mechanism and an incomplete credit set (Cao, Dean, Young, Yazdani and others), so neither is better placed this year. A second weakness is that Ye's separate credit rests on priority details that I recall from memory and that the record has not independently verified; if the committee finds that Ye's role is improvement and not co-origination, the configuration should be revisited rather than defended.

responses.point: Olsson asks, in the chair's first question, what establishes that Ye's contribution is original and decisive and not an improvement of Katori's invention, and she wants JILA results separated from those of Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others.
responses.response: I think the question is the right one and a partial answer is available. Katori's two roles are the 2003 magic-wavelength proposal and the 2005 first demonstration. Ye's group independently built a strontium lattice clock at JILA and evaluated it systematically, combined it with the frequency comb for optical-to-microwave counting, and then led the progression to the 1e-18 level, including the work on many-body interactions and Fermi-degenerate operation, in which the clock stopped being a single-particle device. I would call that a contribution to the physics (how interactions and collisional shifts behave in a lattice clock), not only to the numbers. I accept her caution that the experimental papers carry many authors, and that Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the Oelker-Campbell generation did much of the bench work; the committee should say that the credit is for the group leader who directed and defined the programme, as for any experimental prize. I have not verified the individual dates and would want them checked before a final vote. If the record shows that Ye's role is only refinement, I would prefer Katori alone to a pair that blurs the statutory test.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first and argues that the open pairing mechanism does not weaken the discovery claim, because the correlated insulators and superconducting dome are the robust observation and were predicted by a simple model; the chair asks what evidence would move B024 above B052.
responses.response: I find his distinction between unsettled interpretation and unsettled discovery persuasive in part, and I have moved a little: the existence of the flat-band correlated phases is established and I should not call it premature on the pairing question alone. What still keeps B024 below B052 for me is the credit set, not the physics. The three names include two authors of one theory paper and leave out Cao, the first author of the 2018 experiments, and the contemporaneous Dean, Young, Yazdani and Kim groups. Since a prize is meant to name the people who did the work, I would need a rule that places Cao and one of the other experimental groups credibly, or evidence that the three-name cut is robust, before preferring B024. So my preference rests on attribution and verifiability, not on field type; if the committee finds a defensible set for B024 I would be willing to see it again next year, and it remains my alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B052 with near-identical reasoning to Kroll, and flags with Kroll that the two openings should not be counted as independent evidence; she also treats B035 as the natural precision-measurement companion but declines it as a second part.
responses.response: I agree that our agreement is partly shared reading, and I have tried not to count it. That is why I rest on the physics and on reproducibility. On the chair's question about a two-part prize, I do not see a second part that I would add. B035 would force an arbitrary choice among Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich given Chu's earlier prize and the early interferometers, and combined with B052 it would exceed three people unless one of the lattice-clock names is dropped, which I do not want. I would also second her view that the citation should name the lattice clock explicitly, which answers the question about wording: I regard the 2005 overlap as a drafting matter, not a bar.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is the clearest case of a measurement technique changing what can be observed, in the tradition of the earlier precision-spectroscopy prizes, with the pending redefinition of the second as a consequence.
responses.response: I agree with the conclusion but would give a different argument from his. Tradition and the redefinition of the second are not scientific criteria, as he himself notes that it has not yet happened; the argument that survives is independent agreement across laboratories at 1e-18 and the distinct magic-wavelength idea. I also take up his point that Katori and Ye contribute differently, so the citation must not imply that one only refined the other. The wording I propose, naming invention and realisation, is meant to cover both roles.

uncertainties: Whether the record supports Ye as a co-originator and not as the one who perfected Katori's concept; my dates and the division of work among JILA group members are recalled from memory and unverified.
Whether a possible later nuclear-clock recognition for Ye should affect timing; I think it should not, because the lattice clock is a finished and independent body of work.
How much weight the committee should give to the fundamental-physics payoff, which remains prospective, in deciding that this is a discovery and not an instrument.
Whether other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde and SYRTE, Lisdat, Yb and Hg groups) have claims that would make the two-name set contestable.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist. My Uppsala and Los Alamos links and my work in density functional theory and magnetism do not connect to them, and I have not verified any personal ties beyond my profile. I was the chair for the 2025 prize and am an ordinary member for 2026. I would not recuse from any shortlisted ballot.
